title: Oncall LLM Inference Graph Debugging Cookbook
author: Asha Patel
content:
Summary
-------
This runbook is an on-call focused debugging cookbook for multi-service LLM inference graphs (request router, batching layer, serving runtime, KV cache, model kernels). It prioritizes fast signal-to-action patterns for preserving SLOs (p95 latency, token-cost budget, error-rate) and minimizing blast radius. Use this as your first-response checklist during incidents involving slow or incorrect model responses, token surges, or cascading failures across inference stages.

Scope and objectives
--------------------
- Scope: realtime text generation and chat endpoints served by the Redwood serving runtime and platform routing (hosted & dedicated pools).
- Primary objectives: restore foreground latency SLOs (default: p95 < 300ms), stop token surges, restore correct KV cache behavior, and enable safe rollback of model/kernel changes.
- When to use: triggered by alerts (see Alerting section) or reports from customers indicating timeouts, degraded quality, or cost anomalies.

Ownership and escalation
------------------------
- Triage owner: platform oncall (first responder)
- Escalation: serving-runtime oncall -> runtime-kernel lead -> SRE (if infrastructure: node/GPU issues)
- Pagerduty playbook: "LLM Inference Degradation" -> follow steps below and update incident channel with every major milestone.

Key SLOs and thresholds
------------------------
| Signal | Target | Alert threshold | Pagerduty severity |
|-------|--------|-----------------|-------------------|
| p95 latency (tail) | < 300ms | > 450ms sustained 3m | P1 |
| 5xx / request error rate | < 0.5% | > 2% over 5m | P1 |
| Token throughput vs budget | within baseline | > 2x baseline for 10m | P2 |
| KV cache miss rate (prefix cache) | < 15% | > 40% | P2 |
| Kernel OOMs / preemptions | 0 | > 0.5% per minute | P1 |

Signals and where to check them (quick map)
-------------------------------------------
1) Router & ingress
- Dashboards: "ingress-latency-by-region", "route-fanout-errors"
- Quick checks: request rate, error rate, request payload size distribution (spikes can bypass batching heuristics)
- CLI: curl health endpoint, check API gateway logs for 429s/504s.

2) Batcher / queue layer
- Dashboards: "batch-latency", "batch-size-distribution"
- Quick checks: backlog depth, max wait time, batching policy version (ensure policy matches deployed runtime), consumer lag in queue (Kafka / Redis streams).
- Commands: kafka-consumer-groups --describe or redis-cli XINFO STREAMS <stream>

3) Serving runtime (per-GPU pools)
- Dashboards: "gpu-pool-utilization", "runtime-tail-latency", "kernel-error-rate"
- Quick checks: per-GPU temperature/driver errors, node-level OOMs, container restarts.
- Commands: kubectl -n runtime get pods -o wide | grep <pool>, kubectl logs <pod> -c runtime

4) KV prefix cache and shards
- Dashboards: "kv-cache-hitratio", "kv-cache-latency", "kv-shard-evictions"
- Quick checks: partition skew, eviction storms, degraded replication lag.
- Commands: redis-cli INFO stats, redis-cli CLIENT LIST, check mem_used and instantaneous_ops_per_sec.

5) Model kernel and compilation layer
- Dashboards: "kernel-compile-latency", "jit-fallback-count", "quantization-profile-mismatch"
- Quick checks: recent deploys for kernel or model changes, compilation failures causing fallback slowdowns.
- Commands: check model compile logs in artifacts service and runtime pod logs.

Triage playbook (step-by-step)
------------------------------
1) Stabilize and scope (0–5 min)
  a) Acknowledge the alert in PD and set incident channel.
  b) Run quick smoke: curl /health on router, batcher, and a representative runtime pod. Record HTTP codes and latency.
  c) Identify whether the issue is regional or global by comparing region dashboards.

2) Contain impact (5–15 min)
  a) If token surge: apply rate limiter per-tenant (edge rate-limit rule) to cap offending tenant to baseline.
  b) If batcher backlog high: temporarily lower max_batch_wait_ms or increase consumer parallelism for the impacted pool. Use the rollout API: POST /admin/batcher/config {"max_wait_ms": 20} (change via console if short).
  c) If GPU OOMs: mark nodes unschedulable (cordon) and drain gracefully with eviction window 30s. Use kubectl cordon/drain and autoscaler will rebalance.

3) Deep diagnosis (15–45 min)
  a) Correlate increased latency with KV cache miss spikes. If miss_rate > 40%:
     - Check recent cache flush or shard reassignment (audit log).
     - If eviction storm caused by memory pressure, consider increasing cache memory limit for the shard and triggering a controlled shard rebalance.
  b) If kernel/compile fallbacks observed:
     - Revert recent kernel deployments via canary rollback. Use canary-id and revert in the deployment system.
  c) If request payload sizes increased dramatically:
     - Engage product/CS to validate new client behavior; implement input-size-based throttles or token-limits in the router.

4) Remediation actions (45–90 min)
  a) Emergency model swap: redirect traffic to a validated model variant (lower latency, conservative quantization) using the routing API.
     - POST /admin/routing/switch {"route":"/v1/generate","model":"open-model-v1-safe"}
  b) KV cache rebalance: use operator tool to migrate hot prefixes to additional shards. Follow the operator tool checklist: freeze writes, migrate subset, resume writes.
  c) Apply temporary conservative batching config: reduce batch size cap and reduce wait timers to prioritize latency over throughput.

5) Recovery and verification (90–180 min)
  a) Verify p95 and error-rate trending to normal for 30 minutes.
  b) Remove temporary throttles incrementally and monitor token throughput and cost signals.
  c) Run synthetic replay of representative prompt set (from /evals/playbooks/incident-smoke) to validate correctness and quality regression.

6) Post-incident (after recovery)
  a) Create incident summary in the incident tracker within 24 hours. Include timeline, root cause, mitigations, and follow-ups.
  b) Action items: tag owner and ETA for each follow-up (e.g., kernel regression fix, batcher tuning, alert adjustments).
  c) Schedule a 1-week postmortem review with product and runtime teams if customer impact > 1 hour or P1 breach.

Quick command snippets and checks
--------------------------------
- Check router health: curl -sS -w "%{http_code} %{time_total}\n" https://router.internal/health
- Check batch queue lag (Redis stream): redis-cli XINFO STREAMS /streams/batches | sed -n '1,8p'
- Inspect runtime pod logs for OOM: kubectl -n runtime logs <pod> -c runtime | tail -n 200 | grep -i oom
- Check GPU utilization: kubectl -n runtime exec <pod> -- nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,temperature.gpu --format=csv

Signal -> Immediate action mapping (table)
--------------------------------------
| Signal | Immediate action | Follow-up owner |
|-------|------------------|-----------------|
| p95 > 450ms and batcher backlog high | Reduce max_wait_ms, increase consumer parallelism | platform-oncall + batcher team |
| kv miss_rate spike | Add shard capacity or trigger controlled rebalance | platform-ops |
| kernel compile fallback count rising | Revert kernel deployment to previous stable canary | runtime-team |
| token throughput > 2x baseline | Apply tenant rate-limit & notify customer-success | oncall + customer-success |

Safe rollback and experiment hygiene
-----------------------------------
- Always prefer canary rollback to global rollback. Use the deployment system's canary id and staged rollback command.
- Record rollback reason into deployment metadata.
- After rollback, monitor kernel-compile-ops and model output quality for at least 2 hours.

Alert tuning guidance (for oncall and SRE)
----------------------------------------
- Avoid single-metric alerting. Use composite alerts: p95 > threshold AND batcher backlog > X.
- Use suppression windows for scheduled internal load tests. Tag synthetic traffic with header X-Synthetic: true and suppress alerts accordingly.
- Tune KV miss alerts to avoid sensitivity during known cache maintenance windows.

Playbook for runbook updates and ownership
----------------------------------------
1) If you perform a novel mitigation, update this document with the steps taken and cross-link the incident.
2) Responsible owners should run tabletop for any RI (repeatable incident) discovered by the postmortem.
3) Quarterly review: runtime-team and platform SRE to review top 5 triage workflows and refresh CLI snippets.

-----------------------------------
